constraints: Undo operations are processed one at a time.
The most recently applied non-undone command must be reversed first.

blocks.text: A command commits an inverse record or prior-state record onto a stack. Undo pops exactly the newest applicable record and uses it to restore the preceding state. A queue would expose the oldest change and violate command history. Full replay can be a separate implementation trade-off, but it is not the state discipline requested here. Recursion is unnecessary; the decisive property is LIFO restoration.

messages.text: A queue preserves history, but it restores the oldest retained state first. It becomes appropriate only for oldest-first processing, not Undo.
A retained command log can reconstruct a prior state, but replay does not directly expose and apply the newest undo record as this question requires.
Recursive control flow can use a call stack, but Undo history is directly representable with an explicit stack.

feedback.reason: Undo is newest-first restoration: the last committed unresolved change is the first one that must be reversed.

options.text: Enqueue prior states and restore the oldest state on Undo.
Push one inverse record per command and pop the newest record on Undo.
Retain the full command log and replay the document from its initial state after every Undo.
Use recursion because Undo cannot be represented by an explicit data structure.

prompt: An editor must support repeated Undo so that each request restores the state immediately before the most recent command that has not already been undone. Which retained state directly encodes that access order without replaying earlier commands?

blocks.text: The history entry and the forward mutation form one reversible lifecycle. Information that exists only in the old state must cross the mutation boundary before that state changes.

items: Derive the inverse record from the current pre-change state and the requested forward command.
Push that complete inverse record before changing the current state.
Apply the forward command only after its restoration data is safely retained.
On Undo, pop the newest inverse so the same history entry cannot be consumed twice.
Apply that popped inverse to reconstruct the immediately preceding state.

blocks.text: If a replacement overwrites value X with Y, deriving the inverse afterward may reveal Y but no longer X. Likewise, applying an inverse without popping leaves a stale top that a second Undo could reuse incorrectly.
blocks.title: Post-mutation derivation can be too late

feedback.reason: The inverse must be captured before the forward mutation destroys information needed for restoration; Undo then consumes the newest inverse.

elements.text: Derive the inverse information from the current state and the requested command.
Push that inverse record onto the history stack.
Apply the forward command to produce the new current state.
When Undo is requested, pop the newest inverse record.
Apply the popped inverse record to restore the previous state.

prompt: Order the conceptual steps for safely applying one reversible command and then undoing that same command.

blocks.text: Undo may be disabled, return a defined empty-history result, or perform a documented no-op. What it cannot do is invent a prior state, reuse a record that has already been consumed, or jump to unrelated history. The empty-stack check is a material boundary because a pop requires an existing top record.

messages.text: A sentinel is valid only if the contract deliberately stores one with defined semantics. Fabricating it at the boundary creates a state that was never committed.
A popped inverse has already been consumed. Reusing it violates one-record-per-Undo semantics and can corrupt state.
Oldest-known state is not equivalent to the immediately previous committed state and is not available from an empty stack.

feedback.reason: An empty history stack means there is no previous committed state available through this contract.

options.text: Pop a fabricated sentinel and interpret it as a real prior state.
Restore the oldest state ever observed, even though it is not on the stack.
Return the defined empty-history result and do not pop.
Reuse the inverse record from the previous successful Undo.

prompt: The current state has no committed undo record. The user requests Undo. Which behavior preserves the stack-based history contract?

blocks.text: The committed stack is [A, B, C] with C at the top. Undo pops C first, then B, then A on later requests. Reversing A first would expose queue-like oldest-first behavior and could invalidate later changes that depend on A. This trace diagnoses order semantics, not merely the presence of a collection named history.

messages.text: A is the oldest command. Reversing it first follows FIFO order and can invalidate B and C while they remain applied.
A single Undo consumes one history record unless the command contract explicitly groups changes into one composite record.
B is neither the newest nor the top record; its position does not make it eligible before C.

feedback.reason: The top of the history stack is C, the newest still-applied command.

options.text: Reverse A.
Reverse C.
Reverse B because it is in the middle.
Reverse A, B, and C simultaneously.

prompt: Commands A, B, and C were committed in that order, and none has been undone. Which command must the first Undo reverse?

blocks.text: The logical top remains the newest command. A capacity policy may evict the oldest retained record at the bottom while preserving newest-first Undo among the remaining records. This does not change LIFO semantics for retained entries. It does change how far back Undo can travel, so that product boundary must be explicit.

messages.text: Dropping the new command removes the very record needed for the next Undo and preserves less relevant old history.
Duplicating the new record would make one command appear undoable twice and violates one committed inverse per command.
A stack defines access order, not unbounded retention. Capacity and eviction are separate policies.

feedback.reason: A bounded history preserves the newest reversible states; the stack abstraction does not require retaining every historical record forever.

options.text: Discard the new record so the oldest 100 remain forever.
Ignore the limit because a stack must retain every item ever pushed.
Push two copies of the new record and remove two older records.
Push the new record and discard the oldest retained record.

prompt: An application retains at most the 100 most recent undo records. After a new command is committed while 100 records are already retained, which policy is consistent with bounded Undo history?

blocks.text: Nested savepoints form a containment chain. The deepest active savepoint is the newest unresolved one, so rollback must use the top record. An iterative implementation with an explicit stack preserves the same semantics as recursive call frames. Sorting or FIFO ordering ignores containment and may restore a state outside the failed scope.

messages.text: FIFO restores the outermost or oldest savepoint before the inner failure is resolved.
Recursion is one possible control-flow implementation, but the state rule is explicit LIFO restoration and works iteratively.
State size has no causal relation to nesting order and cannot identify the immediately enclosing savepoint.

feedback.reason: The decisive requirement is restoration of the most recently entered active savepoint, independent of whether control flow is recursive.

options.text: Save active states in LIFO order and restore from the top.
The parser must be written recursively; an iterative parser cannot restore savepoints.
Restore the earliest savepoint first.
Sort savepoints by state size before choosing one.

prompt: A parser records nested savepoints. On failure inside the deepest active savepoint, it must restore the immediately enclosing saved state. Which implementation property is essential?

blocks.text: Undo and redo are usually represented by two stacks. Undo moves a record to redo; a fresh command records its pre-command state on undo and clears redo because replaying the old branch would no longer describe the current document lineage. Earlier undo records remain available.

messages.text: A new command does not invalidate earlier reversible commands that still precede the current state.
Keeping C after a divergent edit would make Redo apply a branch that is no longer based on the current state.
The user has already chosen a new branch; forcing the old command back changes the requested semantics.

feedback.reason: A new command after Undo abandons the old forward branch and creates a new reversible state transition.

options.text: Clear the redo history because D creates a new branch, then push the pre-D state onto the undo stack.
Keep C in redo and append D to the same stack without changing any history.
Clear the undo stack because a new command makes all earlier commands invalid.
Redo C before applying D so the history remains linear.

prompt: An editor supports Undo and Redo. After undoing command C, the user commits a new command D. What history transition is normally required?

blocks.text: The record may be a full snapshot, a diff, or an inverse operation, but its semantic target is the pre-command state. Recording only the post-command state does not identify what to restore unless the command model separately contains an inverse. The order of capture and mutation must be explicit.

messages.text: Repeating a command is not a general inverse and can create another mutation rather than restore S0.
State size says nothing about whether the record represents the correct predecessor.
S1 is the current post-command state, not the predecessor Undo must recover.

feedback.reason: Undo needs the predecessor of the command, so the reversible record must capture S0 or an equivalent inverse before S0 is lost.

options.text: Push S0 or its inverse record before applying the command, then transition to S1.
Push S1 after applying the command; it is always the state Undo must restore.
Push any state with the same size as S0 because size determines reversibility.
Apply the command twice so the second result can reconstruct S0.

prompt: A reversible command changes state from S0 to S1. Which record timing lets Undo restore the state immediately before that command?

blocks.text: If two commits are separate commands, each has a place in the history contract. Deduplicating snapshots would make one Undo silently remove two actions or skip an observable command boundary. A product may intentionally coalesce edits, but that is a separate history policy and must be applied before records enter the stack.

messages.text: An equal snapshot is not an error and does not invalidate earlier history.
Equal output does not prove equal command identity or equal undo semantics.
Skipping a record violates one-Undo-per-retained-transition unless coalescing was explicitly specified.

feedback.reason: Undo history records reversible transitions, not only distinct rendered values; equal snapshots can still represent separate user actions.

options.text: Pop two distinct undo records, even if the visible intermediate text is equal, because command identity and history depth remain distinct.
Keep one record because equal visible text means the commands are the same transition.
Skip the first equal record and undo an older visibly different state.
Clear history whenever two adjacent snapshots have equal values.

prompt: Two consecutive commands happen to produce the same visible document text, but they are distinct commits. What should two Undo actions do?

blocks.text: LIFO access alone is only the ordering half of Undo. The stored snapshot, inverse, or diff must restore the state before the corresponding command, and records must be managed according to explicit capacity and redo policies. Oldest-first is FIFO; unrecorded history cannot be recovered by naming the current top.

messages.text: Once information is discarded, the stack cannot infer it from an unrelated current top without an additional source of history.
Oldest-first conflicts with repeated Undo of the most recent active command.
This is the access order that makes the history a stack.
Undo needs a concrete predecessor or inverse, not just a command count.

feedback.reason: The stack supplies newest-first access, but correctness also requires each record to encode a real predecessor transition.

options.text: Each Undo must reverse the newest change that is still active.
Each retained record identifies the state or inverse needed to restore the predecessor state.
Each Undo must process the oldest change first.
A discarded record can be reconstructed automatically from the current top without any retained information.

prompt: Select all requirements that support storing a process history in a stack for repeated Undo.

blocks.text: Push a snapshot or inverse-operation record before mutation, then apply the action. The exact payload can be a full copy, delta, or command inverse.

messages.text: The old state may already be lost.
Without history, arbitrary mutations cannot generally be reversed.
A snapshot must correspond to a defined state boundary.

feedback.reason: Undo needs a recoverable version of the state that the next action will replace.

options.text: Before applying the new mutation, so the previous state can be restored.
Only after the mutation, when the previous state no longer exists.
Undo can reconstruct every state without stored history.
At an arbitrary time unrelated to the action.

prompt: When implementing undo by snapshots, when should the prior state be saved?

blocks.text: For a set insertion, the inverse may be deletion; for a text edit, it may store the replaced segment. The inverse must contain enough information for the exact contract.

messages.text: Discarding changes is not implementing an undoable mutation.
The post-mutation state may not reveal what changed.
Undo order is recency order, not type order.

feedback.reason: An inverse record can restore the prior state with less memory than a full copy when the mutation is reversible.

options.text: Store the minimal inverse operation or delta needed to restore the prior state.
Store only the current state after mutation and infer the prior state from it.
Sort all actions by type before undoing.
Discard the action so the state never changes.

prompt: What is an alternative to storing a full snapshot for an undoable action?

blocks.text: Underflow can be a no-op with an explicit response, an error, or a disabled command according to the product contract. It must not mutate current state silently.

messages.text: No history does not authorize deleting current state.
Out-of-bounds access is not history.
An invented state is not a prior user state.

feedback.reason: An empty history has no earlier state to restore.

options.text: Expose the contract's no-undo state and leave the current state unchanged.
Clear the current state even though no history exists.
Invent a previous state by repeating the first action.
Read outside the history stack.

prompt: What should an undo command do when no prior state is stored?

blocks.text: The policy must be explicit: a branching history can preserve alternate futures, while a simple two-stack model clears redo on new mutation.

messages.text: Those states no longer describe the current branch without extra branching semantics.
New edits do not imply clearing the document.
History order is action chronology, not type order.

feedback.reason: A new edit after undo creates a new history branch in the usual linear undo/redo model.

options.text: Discard redo states that belong to the abandoned future branch, unless branching history is explicitly supported.
Keep every future state in one linear redo stack regardless of the new edit.
Reset the document to its initial state.
Sort actions chronologically by type.

prompt: What policy is commonly required when a new edit occurs after one or more undos?
